title: Exactly-Once Across a Transactional Boundary
scenario_context: A pipeline reads payment events from a message broker, updates account balances in a relational database, and commits the broker offset — all as part of the same logical operation. The team needs end-to-end exactly-once: each payment must update the balance exactly once regardless of retries.
description: The database and the message broker are separate systems that cannot participate in a single distributed transaction. Which design achieves exactly-once semantics across this two-system boundary?
options: Persist the consumed broker offset inside the same database transaction that updates the balance; on restart, re-read the stored offset rather than relying on the broker's consumer group offset — guaranteeing the offset and balance move atomically
Use at-least-once delivery and add a UNIQUE constraint on `event_id` in the balance update table; duplicate events fail the constraint and are silently discarded
Enable the broker's built-in exactly-once producer setting; this automatically propagates the guarantee through the downstream database write
Use a two-phase commit coordinator that spans both the broker and the database, locking both systems until the transaction is committed on both sides
explanation: When two heterogeneous systems cannot share a transaction, you bring offset tracking into the system that CAN participate in your transaction (the database). Storing the consumed offset in the same DB transaction as the balance update makes both atomic — either both commit or both roll back. On restart, reading the stored offset tells you exactly where to resume, with no risk of re-applying a payment that was already committed. Option B (UNIQUE constraint + discard) works for many cases but relies on the database silently swallowing errors — it can mask real bugs and doesn't handle cases where the event ID is not naturally unique per operation. Option C is incorrect — the broker's exactly-once producer setting applies only to producer → broker, not to downstream database writes. Option D (2PC) is theoretically correct but most message brokers don't support XA transactions and the protocol is fragile and rarely used in practice.
hints: Think about what shared state you could persist in the database so that a restart knows precisely which event was the last successfully processed one.
When two systems cannot share a transaction, the solution is to bring the coordination state entirely inside one of them — the one you can transact against.

title: Duplicate Detection at Scale
scenario_context: A high-volume e-commerce pipeline ingests 50 million order events per day from multiple upstream producers. Due to network retries, approximately 0.1% of events are duplicated. The team needs to deduplicate before computing revenue aggregates. The deduplication window must cover 48 hours (events can arrive up to 48 hours late due to mobile queue draining).
description: Which deduplication strategy offers the best balance of correctness, memory efficiency, and query performance at this scale?
options: Maintain a rolling 48-hour bloom filter (or probabilistic count-min sketch) per event source as a fast first pass, then verify true duplicates against an exact event_id lookup table for the bloom filter's false-positive rate
Store all 50 million event IDs from the past 48 hours in an in-memory hash set; reject any event whose ID is already present
Use a GROUP BY event_id query in the warehouse at query time; aggregate results will automatically deduplicate
Trust upstream producers to deduplicate before sending; add a data quality alert for duplicate rates above 1% but otherwise process all events as received
explanation: At 50M events/day over 48 hours = ~100M event IDs to track. A pure in-memory hash set (Option B) would require ~4-8 GB of RAM depending on UUID length, which is expensive and fragile. A bloom filter reduces memory by 10–50x for a configurable false-positive rate (e.g., 0.01%); the second-pass exact lookup handles only the rare false positives. This two-tier approach is both memory-efficient and correct. Option C (query-time dedup) is only correct for full scans — aggregations over duplicated raw data produce wrong intermediate results. Option D relies on external teams for a correctness guarantee, which violates the pipeline's data quality contract.
hints: Think about the memory requirement for tracking 100 million 128-bit UUIDs in a hash set and whether there's a more space-efficient probabilistic structure.
A probabilistic data structure can give you near-certainty with a fraction of the memory; pairing it with an exact check for its false-positive rate gives you correctness without full memory cost.

title: Delivery Semantics and Consumer-Side State
description: A streaming consumer accumulates a running sum of transaction amounts in an in-memory state store. The broker delivers with at-least-once semantics. A network partition causes the consumer to crash after processing an event but before committing the offset. On restart, the consumer re-reads the event. What is the impact on the running sum, and what is the minimal fix?
options: The running sum is incremented twice for the replayed event (incorrect result); the fix is to make the state update idempotent by storing the last-processed event ID alongside the sum and skipping updates for already-seen IDs
The running sum is not affected because in-memory state is cleared on crash; the consumer starts fresh from the last committed offset, which is correct
The running sum is incremented twice, but this is acceptable because at-least-once semantics explicitly permit double-counting as a known trade-off
The broker detects the duplicate event and filters it before delivery, so the consumer receives each event exactly once despite at-least-once delivery
explanation: With at-least-once delivery, replayed events are re-delivered to the consumer. If the state update (sum += amount) is not idempotent, the replayed event increments the sum a second time, producing an incorrect result. The fix: persist `last_event_id` alongside `running_sum` in the same atomic state update. On restart, if the replayed event's ID matches `last_event_id`, skip the sum update. This makes the state update idempotent without requiring exactly-once from the broker. Option B is wrong — in-memory state is lost on crash, but the event IS re-delivered because the offset wasn't committed. Option C is wrong — double-counting corrupts financial aggregates and is not an acceptable trade-off. Option D is wrong — at-least-once brokers do not filter duplicates on the broker side.
hints: Trace through the crash scenario: the event was processed, the sum was incremented, but the offset commit failed. On restart, what happens when that event is re-delivered?
Making a state transition idempotent means tracking enough context to detect and skip a repeated application of the same transition.

title: Exactly-Once with Fan-Out Sinks
scenario_context: A streaming pipeline reads from a single message broker topic and writes processed results to two downstream sinks: (1) a relational database for operational queries, and (2) an object store for long-term analytics. The pipeline uses at-least-once delivery and must ensure neither sink receives duplicate records.
description: The team wants exactly-once semantics for both sinks. Which design pattern addresses the dual-sink challenge?
options: Write to both sinks inside a single idempotent transaction if both support it; otherwise, designate one sink as primary and use its commit as the offset checkpoint, then replay from the checkpoint to the secondary sink using the primary as the source of truth
Use exactly-once delivery from the broker to the pipeline; the guarantee automatically extends to all downstream sinks without any additional design
Write to the database first; if successful, write to the object store. If the object store write fails, roll back the database write using a compensating transaction
Use separate consumer group offsets for the database sink and the object store sink so each can advance independently, doubling throughput
explanation: The core challenge is that two independent sinks cannot share a single atomic commit. The correct approach: if both sinks support idempotent writes (keyed upserts, conditional puts), each write can be safely retried independently. If not, use the primary sink (database) as the offset anchor and treat the secondary sink (object store) as a derived output that can be reconstructed by replaying from the primary. Option B is wrong — exactly-once delivery from broker to pipeline does not automatically extend to external sinks; each sink's write must be handled independently. Option C (compensating transaction to object store) is fragile — object stores typically don't support rollback semantics and you cannot reliably undo a completed write. Option D (separate offsets) solves ordering but not deduplication — each sink independently replays on failure, still requiring idempotent writes.
hints: Think about what makes committing to two independent systems simultaneously hard: you cannot atomically finish both in a single operation.
When you cannot have a shared atomic commit, the alternative is making each write independently safe to retry — the key word is idempotent.

title: Incident Response: Silent Data Loss
scenario_context: A data engineering team is alerted by a business analyst: the daily revenue report shows $0 for all of yesterday. The pipeline ran without errors and the monitoring dashboard shows all tasks as 'success.' The source database and the warehouse are both healthy.
description: How should the team systematically diagnose a silent zero-revenue day?
options: Start at the output (the report query), verify the mart table contains rows for yesterday, then trace backward through the transformation layers — check row counts at each stage and compare to the previous day to find the first layer where data went to zero
Assume the source database had no transactions yesterday (a business event) and close the incident; the pipeline status shows success so data engineering is not at fault
Re-run the entire pipeline for yesterday immediately; if the report populates correctly, the original run had a transient issue and no further investigation is needed
Check the pipeline logs for any WARNING messages that might indicate soft failures; escalate to infrastructure if no warnings are found
explanation: Silent zero-output with 'success' status is a classic data quality gap: the pipeline ran but produced no meaningful output. The systematic approach is backward tracing with row-count auditing: (1) verify the mart table has zero rows or incorrect aggregates for yesterday; (2) check the staging layer; (3) check raw ingestion; (4) check the source. The first layer where rows disappear or drop to zero identifies the root cause — a broken filter, an empty partition, a JOIN with no matches, or a failed ingestion. Option B (assume a business event) skips diagnosis. Option C (immediate re-run) may restore data but doesn't diagnose root cause — the problem will recur. Option D (check WARNING logs) is narrow; silent failures often produce no warnings.
hints: When a pipeline succeeds but produces empty output, the bug is often a silent data filter, a JOIN that matches nothing, or a partition that was never written — none of which raise exceptions.
Row count auditing at each stage turns a 'where did the data go?' question into a 'which stage reduced the count to zero?' question with a definitive answer.

title: Incident Response: Cascading Pipeline Failures
scenario_context: A data platform has 80 downstream pipelines that all depend on a single upstream ingestion job. The upstream job starts failing due to a schema change in the source system. Within 2 hours, 65 of the 80 downstream jobs have failed because they can't find expected columns in the upstream output table.
description: The team must contain the incident and prevent further propagation. What is the correct triage order?
options: First, pause the upstream job to stop producing invalid output; notify owners of the 15 still-running downstream jobs to halt them proactively; then fix the schema change at the ingestion layer before restarting anything, beginning with the upstream job, then downstream jobs in dependency order
Fix the downstream jobs first, since they are the majority of failures and each team can patch their own job independently without waiting for the upstream fix
Restart all failed downstream jobs simultaneously with increased retry counts so they can recover when the upstream issue is resolved
Roll back the source system's schema change to unblock the ingestion job immediately, then investigate the schema change in a staging environment without time pressure
explanation: The correct incident response for a cascading failure is: (1) stop the bleeding — pause the upstream job that is generating invalid output so the 15 remaining downstream jobs don't also fail; (2) communicate — alert downstream teams proactively before they discover failures; (3) fix root cause — correct the schema handling in the ingestion layer; (4) restart in dependency order — upstream first, then downstream, to avoid starting consumers before their dependencies are healthy. Option B (fix downstream first) is inefficient — fixing 80 symptoms without fixing the root cause means they'll break again on the next ingestion run. Option C (simultaneous restart with retries) generates noise and wastes compute while the root cause exists. Option D (roll back source schema) may not be feasible if the source system is a production database owned by another team.
hints: In a cascading failure, the most important first action is stopping further propagation — what change prevents additional downstream jobs from entering the failure state?
Fixing symptoms (downstream jobs) before fixing the root cause (upstream ingestion) means the symptoms return on the next run.

title: Incident Response: Data Corruption in Production
scenario_context: A data engineer discovers that a transformation bug introduced 10 days ago has been silently writing incorrect `customer_segment` values to the warehouse. Downstream teams have been using these incorrect segments for marketing campaigns and financial reports. The bug is now fixed.
description: The team must decide how to handle the corrupted historical data. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Reprocess the last 10 days using the fixed pipeline, atomically replacing the corrupted partitions; notify all downstream consumers of the data issue and the reprocessing window so they can re-pull corrected data and flag any business decisions made on corrupted data
Leave the historical data as-is to avoid disrupting downstream consumers; let them know the segment values after the fix date are correct and they should only trust future data
Silently reprocess the last 10 days without notifying downstream teams; they will naturally get correct data when they next query the warehouse
Archive the corrupted data for audit purposes and create new tables with corrected values; keep both versions available so downstream teams can choose which to use
explanation: Data corruption incidents require both technical remediation and stakeholder communication. Atomically replacing the corrupted partitions via backfill fixes the technical problem. Notifying downstream consumers is equally critical: they may have business decisions, ML model training runs, or financial reports already based on wrong data that need to be re-evaluated. Option B (leave history as-is) leaves corrupted data in place, which will continue to mislead consumers who query historical periods. Option C (silent reprocess) is dangerous — downstream teams may not notice the change and may have downstream artifacts (trained models, reports) derived from the corrupted data that still need correction. Option D (two tables) creates long-term confusion and doesn't guarantee downstream teams use the correct version.
hints: Think about the two dimensions of the problem: the corrupted data in the warehouse itself, and the downstream artifacts (reports, models, decisions) that were built on it.
A silent fix corrects the warehouse but leaves downstream teams unaware that their existing artifacts may still reflect the corrupted values.

title: Lineage for Impact Analysis
scenario_context: A data platform team wants to decommission an old source table `legacy_orders`. Before doing so, they need to know every downstream table, report, and machine learning feature that depends on it, directly or transitively.
description: Which combination of lineage practices makes this impact analysis feasible and reliable?
options: Maintain automated column-level lineage that captures both direct dependencies (tables that JOIN to `legacy_orders`) and transitive dependencies (tables that join to those tables), enabling a full downstream impact graph to be queried before decommissioning
Search the codebase for string literals containing 'legacy_orders' using grep; any file that references the table name is a dependent
Ask each team that owns downstream tables to manually audit whether their pipelines use `legacy_orders`; compile responses before decommissioning
Decommission the table and monitor for failures over the next 48 hours; any pipeline that fails is a dependent and can be restored from backup
explanation: Automated lineage (column-level or table-level) builds a dependency graph that can be traversed forward from `legacy_orders` to enumerate all direct and transitive consumers. This is the only reliable method for large platforms with hundreds of tables. Option B (grep) misses dependencies expressed through dynamic SQL, configuration files, or intermediate views. It also misses transitive dependencies (table A uses `legacy_orders`; table B uses table A — grep for `legacy_orders` in B's code finds nothing). Option C (manual audit) is unreliable at scale — teams may not know all their own transitive dependencies. Option D (decommission and watch for failures) is destructive and risks breaking production workloads.
hints: Think about the difference between direct references (in code) and transitive dependencies (table A depends on table B which depends on the source) — which approach handles both?
Automated lineage graphs can be traversed programmatically; manual or code-search approaches cannot reliably follow chains of dependencies.

title: Observability: Distinguishing Pipeline vs Data Quality Issues
scenario_context: A revenue dashboard shows a 30% drop in yesterday's revenue compared to the same day last week. The pipeline completed successfully and all technical health checks are green. The business team escalates it as a potential data issue.
description: Which observability signals would allow the data team to quickly distinguish a genuine business revenue drop from a data quality or pipeline issue?
options: Compare row counts, null rates on revenue columns, and source record counts at the ingestion layer against historical baselines for the same weekday; cross-reference with a separate operational metric (e.g., transaction count from the source system) that the pipeline does not control
Check the pipeline execution logs for any ERROR or WARNING messages; if none are found, conclude the revenue drop is a business event and close the ticket
Re-run the pipeline for yesterday; if the output is the same, it's a data issue; if different, it's a pipeline non-determinism issue
Ask the business team to verify with their CRM whether sales were actually lower yesterday; data engineering should not speculate about business metrics
explanation: Distinguishing a business event from a pipeline issue requires independent corroborating signals. Key checks: (1) row counts at ingestion — did fewer records arrive from the source? (2) null rates on revenue columns — are revenue values present? (3) comparison with a source-system operational metric (transaction counts, API logs) that your pipeline doesn't touch. If the source metric also shows 30% fewer transactions, it's likely a genuine business event. If source metrics are normal but ingestion row counts are low, it's a pipeline issue. Option B (check ERROR logs) misses the 'silent failure' class of bugs. Option C (re-run) works for non-determinism detection but not for diagnosing root cause. Option D (defer to business team) abdicates the data team's responsibility to diagnose technical pipeline issues.
hints: Think about what evidence would definitively point to 'the data was never ingested' versus 'the data arrived but was computed incorrectly' versus 'less revenue actually occurred'.
An independent signal from the source system that your pipeline doesn't control is the key to distinguishing a pipeline failure from a real business event.

title: SCD Type 2 and Fact Table Joins
scenario_context: A retail data warehouse uses a SCD Type 2 `dim_customer` table. A fact table `fact_orders` stores historical orders, each with a `customer_sk` (surrogate key) pointing to the dim_customer row that was current at order time. A business analyst wants to see orders alongside the customer's segment as it was when each order was placed.
description: Which query pattern correctly retrieves the historical segment for each order?
options: Join `fact_orders` to `dim_customer` on `customer_sk` directly — the surrogate key already points to the exact version of the customer record that was current when the order was placed
Join `fact_orders` to `dim_customer` on `natural_key` (e.g., `customer_id`) and filter `WHERE is_current = TRUE` to get the latest segment
Join `fact_orders` to `dim_customer` on `customer_id = customer_id AND order_date BETWEEN effective_from AND COALESCE(effective_to, '9999-12-31')` to find the version active at order time
Join `fact_orders` to `dim_customer` on `natural_key` and take the maximum surrogate key per customer_id to identify the most recent version
explanation: The SCD Type 2 pattern assigns a unique surrogate key (`customer_sk`) to each version row. The fact table stores the surrogate key that was current at transaction time, not the natural key. Therefore, `fact_orders.customer_sk = dim_customer.customer_sk` directly resolves to the exact historical version without any date range logic. Option B retrieves the *current* segment, not the historical segment — it would show today's segment for all past orders. Option C uses a date range join on the natural key, which works but is more expensive than the surrogate key join and is only necessary if the fact table stores the natural key (an anti-pattern). Option D retrieves the most recent version, not the version at order time.
hints: Think about why the data warehouse assigns a surrogate key to each version row rather than just using the customer's natural ID.
The surrogate key encodes 'which version of this customer was active at this point in time' — following it directly to the dimension row gives you the correct historical snapshot.

title: SCD Type 2 and Late-Arriving Dimension Changes
scenario_context: A retail warehouse loads customer dimension changes nightly via CDC. Yesterday, a data pipeline bug delayed the ingestion of a customer segment change that actually occurred 3 days ago. The fact table contains 3 days of orders pointing to the old customer_sk (the pre-change version). The corrected change has now been applied to the dimension table.
description: What is the most correct remediation for the affected fact table records?
options: Update the `customer_sk` in the affected fact table rows to reference the correct version of the customer (the one that was actually active at order time); this requires knowing the correct effective dates of the delayed dimension change
Leave the fact table unchanged and add a correction note in the data dictionary; historical data should never be modified to preserve audit integrity
Delete the affected fact rows and reload them from the source transaction system to ensure they reference the correct customer version
Create a new corrected dimension row with a backdated `effective_from` and update all future queries to use a date-range join instead of surrogate key join
explanation: Late-arriving dimension changes are a known SCD Type 2 challenge. The correct fix: insert the delayed dimension row with the correct `effective_from` date (3 days ago) and `effective_to` date, then update the `customer_sk` in the affected fact rows to point to this correctly-dated row. This restores historical accuracy. Option B (leave unchanged) preserves incorrect data permanently, which fails both accuracy and compliance requirements. Option C (delete and reload) is expensive, potentially disruptive to production, and only works if the source system retains the transaction records. Option D (backdated row + query change) is partially correct for the dimension but changing all queries to date-range joins breaks the surrogate key pattern and is not scalable.
hints: The core problem is that fact rows reference the wrong dimension version. What targeted change to the fact table would make them reference the right version?
SCD Type 2 corrections require both inserting the delayed dimension row with correct effective dates and re-pointing the fact rows that fell in that time window.

title: Schema Evolution with Columnar Storage
scenario_context: A data lake stores 3 years of Parquet files. The team needs to add a new `geo_region` column to a table with 50,000 Parquet files. The column will be NULL for all historical records (no backfill). The team must not break existing readers during or after the change.
description: Which approach correctly adds the new column while preserving backward and forward compatibility for both old and new readers?
options: Update the table schema metadata in the catalog (e.g., Iceberg or Hive Metastore) to include `geo_region` as a nullable column; existing Parquet files are not rewritten — readers that understand schema evolution will return NULL for `geo_region` when reading old files that lack the column
Rewrite all 50,000 existing Parquet files to include a NULL `geo_region` column so that all files have a uniform schema before any readers are updated
Create a new table with the updated schema and migrate readers to the new table; maintain the old table in read-only mode for legacy consumers
Add `geo_region` as a new Parquet file alongside the existing files; readers must union the two file sets to reconstruct the full schema
explanation: Modern table formats (Iceberg, Delta Lake) support schema evolution at the metadata layer: adding a nullable column updates the schema in the catalog without touching existing data files. Readers that understand the table format return NULL for missing columns in old files. This is efficient (no file rewrites), compatible (old readers that don't know about `geo_region` can still read the files — they just don't see the new column), and correct (new readers get NULL for old records). Option B (rewrite all files) is expensive — 50,000 file rewrites for a single NULL column addition is unnecessary. Option C (new table + migration) is too disruptive for a simple nullable column addition. Option D is not a valid approach — Parquet files are self-contained; you cannot 'add' a column as a separate file.
hints: Think about where the schema is authoritatively defined in a modern table format: in each individual file, or in a separate catalog/metadata layer?
When the schema lives in the metadata layer and new columns are nullable, existing files remain valid — readers simply use the default (NULL) for rows from files that predate the column.

title: Breaking Schema Change with Active Consumers
scenario_context: A streaming system has 12 consumer services reading from a topic encoded with schema version v3. The engineering team needs to deploy schema version v4, which removes two deprecated fields and changes the type of one existing field. Consumers cannot all be updated simultaneously — deployments take 3 days.
description: How should the team manage this breaking schema change with zero consumer downtime?
options: Publish v4 events to a new topic while continuing to publish v3 events to the old topic; update consumers one by one to read from the new topic; once all consumers are on v4, deprecate the old topic — the dual-publish window is 3 days
Push v4 to all consumers as a forced upgrade over 24 hours; the 3-day rollout is too slow for a breaking change and creates schema inconsistency between producers and consumers
Add a schema version header to each message and have consumers read the header to decide how to deserialize; both v3 and v4 logic lives in every consumer simultaneously

Convert the type change to a non-breaking change by making the field accept both the old and new type as a union type, then add the deprecated fields back as optional nulls, making v4 technically backward-compatible
explanation: Dual-topic publishing is the standard approach for breaking changes with staggered consumer upgrades. The producer publishes identical events to both the v3 topic (for consumers not yet upgraded) and the v4 topic (for upgraded consumers). This gives each consumer team a 3-day window to upgrade independently without service disruption. The dual-publish overhead is temporary and bounded. Option B (forced 24-hour upgrade) is the fastest approach but creates operational risk — a failed deployment on any of the 12 services disrupts that consumer immediately. Option C (version header in consumer) is complex to maintain — having two deserialization code paths in every consumer long-term creates technical debt. Option D (make v4 backward-compatible) fundamentally changes what v4 is — if you keep deprecated fields and relax type changes, you haven't made a breaking change; the scenario requires the breaking change be deployed.
hints: The core constraint is: some consumers will be on v3 while others are on v4 simultaneously. What architecture allows both to coexist without conflict?
Separate communication channels (topics) for each schema version allow the producer to serve both audiences simultaneously with no serialization conflicts.

title: Cost Optimization: Materialization Decisions
scenario_context: A data platform runs 500 analyst queries per day on a raw events table (2 TB, 50 billion rows). The top 5 query patterns together account for 80% of compute spend. Each of these patterns performs the same expensive 3-table JOIN and filters on `event_date`. The remaining 20% of queries are highly varied and exploratory.
description: Which materialization strategy minimizes total compute cost while preserving full ad-hoc query capability?
options: Materialize the 3-table JOIN result (filtered by the common date range) as a pre-aggregated or pre-joined summary table for the 5 common patterns; keep the raw table available for the 20% of exploratory queries — the 80/20 split justifies targeted materialization
Materialize all possible query result combinations using a complete cube; exploratory queries will then always hit a pre-computed result regardless of their filters
Cache all query results in a distributed cache with a 24-hour TTL; repeated queries within the cache window pay zero compute cost
Increase the warehouse cluster size during peak hours so the expensive JOINs run faster; total compute spend decreases because each query completes in less time
explanation: Targeted materialization covers the 80% high-cost patterns with pre-computed results while leaving the raw table intact for ad-hoc exploration. The 5 common patterns share the same expensive JOIN, so materializing it once amortizes the cost across all 400 daily executions. The remaining 100 exploratory queries access the raw table, which is acceptable since they represent only 20% of spend. Option B (full cube) is exponentially expensive to compute and maintain for a table with many dimensions — it's only practical for a small number of fixed dimensions. Option C (query cache) is effective for identical repeated queries but fails for ad-hoc exploration (every unique query is a cache miss). Option D (larger cluster) is counterproductive — it increases cost because you pay for larger instance types; faster execution alone does not reduce cost unless it allows the cluster to be shut down sooner.
hints: Think about the relationship between query frequency and the marginal value of pre-computing: which queries benefit most from materialization?
Pre-computing the expensive common JOIN once per day is far cheaper than executing the same JOIN 400 times per day on the raw data.

title: Cost Optimization: Partition Strategy and Scan Cost
scenario_context: A marketing team queries a 10 TB behavioral events table. 90% of queries filter by `user_cohort` (10 distinct values) and `event_date` (last 30 days). The remaining 10% of queries scan full historical ranges without cohort filters. The table is currently unpartitioned and costs $8,000/month in scan compute.
description: Which partitioning strategy best balances cost reduction for the 90% case while remaining performant for the 10% case?
options: Partition by `event_date` (day-level) and use clustering/sorting by `user_cohort` within each partition — date partitioning prunes irrelevant days for the 90% case while sorting accelerates cohort filters without creating too many partitions; full scans in the 10% case still benefit from date pruning
Partition by `user_cohort` first, then by `event_date` — cohort partitioning gives perfect isolation for the 90% case and date sub-partitioning further prunes the range
Partition by `event_date` at the hour level to maximize pruning granularity; each query scans the smallest possible set of files
Partition by a composite key of `(user_cohort, event_date, event_type)` — the highest-cardinality composite partition enables maximum pruning for any query combination
explanation: Date partitioning with cohort clustering is the right balance: (1) date pruning benefits both the 90% case (last 30 days) and the 10% case (any date range filter is common in historical scans); (2) sorting/clustering by `user_cohort` within partitions allows the query engine to skip row groups that don't match the cohort filter — effective for 90% of queries without the partition overhead of a separate cohort dimension. Option B (cohort first, then date) creates only 10 top-level cohort partitions, which provides some pruning for the 90% case, but the 10% case (full historical scan without cohort filter) must read all 10 cohort partitions — no pruning benefit. Also, over a multi-year history, the nested date partitions would be very numerous. Option C (hour-level date) creates 24x more partitions per day, causing small-file problems and excessive metadata overhead for scans that span many hours. Option D (composite 3-key partition) creates extremely high partition cardinality (10 cohorts × 365 days × N event types), causing a severe small-file problem.
hints: Think about which dimension appears in the most queries and benefits both the 90% and 10% case — that should be the primary partition key.
High-cardinality composite partition keys create too many small files; clustering within a partition achieves similar pruning benefits without multiplying file count.

title: Watermark and Out-of-Order Event Storms
scenario_context: A streaming pipeline processes IoT sensor readings. Under normal conditions, events arrive within 5 seconds of their event_time. The watermark is set to 10 seconds. Periodically, network batch uploads from offline sensors dump 1,000 events with event_times from 2 hours ago. The late events cause all currently active windows to be closed prematurely because the watermark jumps backward — or so the team believes.
description: What actually happens when a batch of events with very old timestamps arrives, and what is the correct design response?
options: Watermarks can only advance, never go backward — the old-timestamp events are dropped as 'late' since the watermark has already passed their event_time; the correct response is to route these late events to a side output for separate reprocessing or batch correction
The watermark jumps backward to accommodate the old timestamps, reopening closed windows and recomputing results — this is the intended behavior of event-time processing
The late events are held in state indefinitely until a manual operator command advances the watermark past them, causing unbounded state growth until the command is issued
The streaming framework detects the late-arriving batch and automatically adjusts the watermark tolerance for that sensor's partition to cover 2 hours of lateness going forward
explanation: A fundamental property of watermarks is monotonicity: the watermark only advances forward. Events with event_times earlier than the current watermark are classified as 'late' and are dropped (or routed to a side output) — they do not cause the watermark to go backward or reopen closed windows. This is by design: rewinding the watermark would require reopening windows and recomputing results, which has unbounded state costs. The correct architecture routes late events to a side output (a separate stream or table) for separate handling — either a delayed batch correction or accumulation for later batch reprocessing. Option B incorrectly describes watermark behavior. Option C is wrong — late events don't block the watermark. Option D is incorrect — watermarks don't auto-adjust per-partition for detected late batches.
hints: Think about whether a streaming engine's notion of 'how far along in event time we are' can ever move backward — and what that means for events that arrive very late.
The design question for periodic late-arriving batches is not how to accommodate them inline, but what separate path handles events that arrive after their window has definitively closed.

title: Watermark Tuning for Multi-Source Joins
scenario_context: A streaming pipeline joins two streams: a click event stream (events arrive within 1 second of event_time) and an impression event stream (events arrive within 20 seconds of event_time due to ad server batching). The pipeline joins clicks to impressions within a 5-minute event-time window. The current watermark is set to 2 seconds on both streams.
description: Clicks are correctly joined, but ~40% of impressions are dropped as late before the join can complete. What is the correct fix?
options: Set the watermark on the impression stream to 30 seconds (to cover the 20-second delay with a buffer) while keeping the click stream watermark at 2 seconds — stream-stream joins in modern frameworks support per-stream watermarks, and the join engine waits for the slower stream's watermark to advance before closing the join window
Increase both stream watermarks to 30 seconds so the join engine waits equally long on both sides before closing any join window
Switch the impression stream to processing-time semantics to avoid the late-event problem; only the click stream needs event-time semantics for the join
Reduce the join window from 5 minutes to 30 seconds so fewer impressions are required to arrive within the window
explanation: In a stream-stream join, the engine needs both sides to have advanced their watermarks past the join window's end before the window can be closed. Setting the impression stream watermark to 30 seconds (covering its 20-second delay) allows the engine to wait appropriately for late impressions without holding the join open indefinitely. Modern frameworks like Flink support per-stream watermarks. Option B (both to 30s) works but unnecessarily delays the click side, adding 28 seconds of latency to an already-fast stream. Option C (processing time for impressions) breaks the event-time join semantics — a click at 10:00:01 and an impression at 10:00:02 (but processed at 10:00:22 due to batching) would not be matched in the same event-time window. Option D (shorter window) doesn't fix the problem — the issue is watermark delay, not window size.
hints: Think about what determines when the engine considers a given event-time window closed for each individual stream — and why two streams with different arrival latency profiles need different settings.
For a stream-stream join, each stream's allowed lateness should reflect that stream's actual delivery characteristics — not a one-size-fits-all setting.

title: Lakehouse ACID and Concurrent Writes
scenario_context: A data lakehouse (using a table format like Apache Iceberg) has a nightly batch job that rewrites and compacts a large partition and a real-time streaming job that continuously appends new rows to the same partition. Both run concurrently.
description: What consistency problem can arise, and how does the table format's ACID model prevent it?
options: Without ACID, the compaction job could overwrite files that the streaming job is actively appending to, corrupting data or losing rows. ACID-compliant table formats use optimistic concurrency control: both jobs write to separate file sets, and the catalog uses atomic metadata commits with conflict detection — if both try to modify the same partition metadata simultaneously, one is retried
ACID in a lakehouse context only prevents read-write conflicts; concurrent write-write conflicts between batch and streaming jobs always require a distributed lock manager
The streaming job must be paused during compaction to prevent conflicts; ACID does not cover concurrent write operations, only concurrent reads
Lakehouse ACID guarantees prevent all conflicts by serializing all writes through a single writer coordinator, which inherently prevents concurrent write throughput
explanation: Lakehouse table formats (Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi) use optimistic concurrency control at the metadata layer. Each writer (batch compaction or streaming append) reads the current snapshot, makes its changes (writing new data files), then attempts an atomic metadata commit. If two writers modified the same partition concurrently, the second commit detects the conflict and can retry (in the case of non-overlapping operations like append + compaction on different row sets, many formats can resolve conflicts automatically; for true overlapping writes, one writer retries). This is fundamentally different from a database's pessimistic locking. Option B is incorrect — lakehouse ACID covers write-write conflicts via metadata-level CAS (compare-and-swap). Option C is incorrect — ACID does cover concurrent writes, which is the primary motivation for adopting lakehouse formats. Option D is incorrect — a single writer coordinator would be a performance bottleneck; optimistic concurrency avoids this.
hints: Think about how a file-system-based storage layer differs from a relational database in terms of atomicity: what happens without a coordination mechanism when two jobs write to the same logical partition?
Optimistic concurrency assumes conflicts are rare and resolves them at commit time rather than preventing concurrent access — this is what makes lakehouse formats both correct and high-throughput.

title: Data Lake Zone Architecture Trade-offs
scenario_context: A company is designing a data lake architecture. They must support: (1) raw data preservation for regulatory compliance (7-year retention), (2) fast iterative data science experimentation, (3) reliable production reporting with strict SLAs, and (4) cost efficiency at 10 PB scale.
description: Which multi-zone architecture best addresses all four requirements?
options: Three zones: raw (immutable, compressed, cold-tiered after 90 days), curated (cleaned, typed, partitioned, hot for production SLAs), and sandbox (ephemeral, short-TTL, cheap instance types for data science experimentation) — production jobs read only from curated; data scientists work in sandbox without impacting production
Two zones: raw (all incoming data) and gold (fully refined production tables); data scientists query the gold tables directly to ensure they use production-quality data
Single zone with row-level access controls: all data in one place with permissions governing who can read what; data engineers, scientists, and analysts all query the same tables

Four zones: landing (unvalidated raw), bronze (validated raw), silver (transformed), gold (aggregated) — every dataset must progress through all four zones before being queryable, ensuring consistent quality
explanation: The three-zone architecture addresses all four requirements: (1) the raw zone preserves original data immutably for compliance, with cold tiering for cost after 90 days; (2) the sandbox zone gives data scientists ephemeral, cheap compute without read locks or SLA risk on production data; (3) the curated zone is partitioned and hot-tiered for the strict production SLA; (4) cold tiering of raw data and ephemeral sandboxes manage 10 PB cost. Option B (two zones) forces data scientists to query production tables, creating resource contention that threatens production SLAs. Option C (single zone) creates resource contention and makes it hard to provide separate cost and performance profiles. Option D (four mandatory zones) is bureaucratically rigid — requiring every dataset to pass through all four zones creates unnecessary latency for exploratory data that doesn't need gold-quality processing.
hints: Think about the four requirements as potentially competing forces: compliance (immutable raw), experimentation (iterative, ephemeral), production (reliable, SLA-bound), and cost (tiering, right-sizing) — does a single or two-zone architecture serve all four simultaneously?
Isolation between production and experimental workloads is a key design principle: data scientists experimenting on production tables create resource contention that threatens SLAs.

title: Data Quality at Scale: Statistical Anomaly Detection
scenario_context: A financial data platform processes 200 daily feeds from external data vendors. Each feed has different volume characteristics — some are 100 rows/day, others are 10 million rows/day. A simple threshold (e.g., row count < 1000 = alert) doesn't work because it misses small feeds that drop from 100 to 10 rows and creates false positives for large feeds that legitimately vary by 20%.
description: Which data quality monitoring design handles heterogeneous feed volumes correctly?
options: Train a per-feed anomaly model (e.g., Z-score against a rolling 30-day baseline, or a seasonal decomposition model for feeds with day-of-week patterns) that alerts when the current count falls outside a statistically significant band relative to that feed's own historical behavior
Set a universal percentage threshold (e.g., alert if today's count is <50% of the 7-day average) applied uniformly to all feeds; this normalizes for volume differences
Only monitor the 20 largest feeds by row count; small feeds represent low data volume and therefore low risk to downstream consumers
Alert on all row count changes of any magnitude and route alerts to feed owners for manual triage; data quality is too context-dependent to automate
explanation: Per-feed statistical models handle heterogeneous volumes correctly: each feed's baseline is learned from its own history, so a 90% drop on a 100-row feed (10 rows) and a 90% drop on a 10M-row feed (1M rows) are both detected as anomalies relative to their respective baselines. Seasonal decomposition handles feeds that legitimately have day-of-week patterns (e.g., weekday feeds that drop to 0 on weekends). Option B (universal percentage threshold) is better than a fixed threshold but still fails for feeds with legitimate high variance (20% daily fluctuation causes false positives) or for the small feed dropping from 100 to 10 (which is 90% and would correctly alert, but a 20% drop on a low-volume feed might not — the percentage must be calibrated per feed). Option C (only large feeds) ignores that even small feeds can trigger cascading downstream failures if they are join keys for larger tables. Option D (alert on all changes) generates alert fatigue and requires human triage for every normal daily variation.
hints: The challenge is that 'normal' means different things for each feed — a 20% variation might be expected noise for one feed and a major anomaly for another.
A model that learns each feed's own history produces feed-specific baselines, making the alerting threshold relative to what is actually normal for that feed.

title: Data Contract Breach During Peak Traffic
scenario_context: At 8:47 PM on the highest-traffic night of the year, a producer team deploys a breaking schema change to a high-volume Kafka topic without communicating it in advance and without going through the schema registry. The change removes a required field (discount_amount) and renames another (item_id → product_id). Three downstream consumers are active at the time: Consumer A — a real-time order aggregation job that has been running for 23 minutes since the bad messages began, and is currently writing NULL discount_amount values into the orders mart; Consumer B — a fraud detection pipeline that deserialized one bad message, raised an exception, and halted with no data written; Consumer C — an overnight batch job scheduled to start in 4 hours that reads from the compacted topic. The on-call data engineer must choose the correct sequence of remediation actions.
description: What is the correct triage order to contain the damage, restore contract compliance, and repair affected data with the minimum blast radius?
options: Option A — Quarantine Consumer A immediately by blocking its writes to the orders mart for the suspect 23-minute window → trigger rollback of the producer schema change → replay Consumer A from the Kafka offset just before the first bad message → resume Consumer B (it crashed cleanly, no bad data landed, so resume is sufficient after rollback) → allow Consumer C to proceed at its scheduled time against the now-corrected topic.

Option B — Trigger rollback of the producer schema change first, then replay Consumer A's 23-minute bad window, then resume Consumer B, then quarantine the bad rows in the orders mart as a post-cleanup step. Consumer A's writes can continue during the rollback window since the rollback will happen quickly.

Option C — Immediately replay all three consumers from their last committed checkpoint, then trigger the producer rollback, then quarantine any suspect mart data identified after replay. Replaying before rollback ensures no consumer falls further behind while the rollback is negotiated with the producer team.

Option D — Alert the producer team and wait for them to acknowledge and revert the change before taking any consumer-side action. Scale down Consumer A to one replica in the meantime to reduce the volume of bad rows entering the orders mart while the rollback is coordinated.
explanation:
Option A is correct. The right remediation order for a contract breach with active data corruption is always: Contain → Restore contract → Replay bad window → Resume unaffected consumers.

Quarantine first, not rollback: Consumer A is actively writing NULL discount_amount values into the orders mart every second. Even if the producer rollback takes only five minutes, that is five more minutes of corrupt rows accumulating. A write-block on the orders mart for the suspect window costs nothing and immediately halts the blast radius from growing. The quarantine does not delete the rows — it marks the window as under repair so downstream reads can be suppressed while the fix is applied.

Rollback before replay: Replaying Consumer A against a still-broken schema would produce the same corrupt output again. The producer schema must be restored first so that messages flowing through the topic conform to the original contract before any consumer attempts to re-consume them.

Consumer-specific triage, not blanket replay: Consumer B crashed on the first bad message and wrote nothing — it needs only a resume after rollback. Consumer C has not started — it will read the corrected topic at its scheduled time with no special handling. Only Consumer A has a window of bad data that requires replay. A blanket replay-all strategy wastes compute, extends the recovery window, and risks introducing new errors in pipelines that did not need repair.

Option B omits the quarantine step. Consumer A continues writing corrupt data during the rollback window — potentially 5–10 minutes of additional NULL rows at peak traffic volume. Quarantining bad rows as a post-cleanup step after replay is both later and more expensive than blocking writes at the start.

Option C replays all consumers before rolling back the schema. Replaying Consumer A against the broken schema produces the same bad output again. Consumer B and Consumer C do not need replay at all. This option inverts the entire priority order.

Option D delegates the rollback to the producer team and waits. In an active incident with data corruption in production at peak traffic, waiting is not an option — it is the failure mode. The on-call engineer should use the schema registry to force-revert the schema version, or coordinate the rollback directly. Scaling down to one replica reduces the volume of bad rows but does not stop the corruption; it is a half-measure that still allows corrupt data to accumulate.
hints: When a consumer is actively writing corrupt data, the first priority is stopping more bad rows from entering production — before the root cause is fixed. Which action immediately halts the blast radius without requiring coordination with the producer team?
Replay is only safe after the source schema is restored. If you replay Consumer A while the broken schema is still active in the topic, what does the replay produce?

Each consumer has a different damage state: one wrote bad data for 23 minutes, one crashed cleanly with nothing written, one has not started. Triage each independently — a blanket action applied to all three wastes time and can introduce new errors in pipelines that did not need repair.

title: Snowflake Warehouse Cost Optimization: Separate Warehouses and Auto-Suspend
scenario_context:
A company's Snowflake spend has grown to $45,000/month. All workloads share a single X-Large warehouse (16 credits/hour, auto-suspend disabled). Usage analysis shows three distinct workload patterns:
  - Analyst ad-hoc queries: 20–30 bursts/day, 2–5 min each, business hours only (8 AM–6 PM)
  - Overnight dbt batch runs: 4 jobs/night, each 45–90 min, 10 PM–4 AM
  - BI dashboard refresh: every 5 min, 15–30 sec each, 7 AM–9 PM

The warehouse idles for roughly 9 hours/day (nights after batch + weekends). Credits are $3.00 each.
description: Which warehouse configuration reduces cost the most while maintaining performance isolation between workloads?
options: Split into three warehouses sized for each workload: (1) Analyst — L (8 credits/hr), auto-suspend 5 min; (2) Batch — XL (16 credits/hr), auto-suspend 10 min, scheduled resume at 10 PM; (3) BI — XS (1 credit/hr), auto-suspend 2 min — estimated savings: ~60% vs current flat-rate XL with no suspend

Keep the single XL warehouse but enable auto-suspend at 60 minutes — the warehouse will suspend during the nightly idle and resume automatically for each workload, cutting cost roughly proportional to the idle fraction

Downsize the single warehouse from XL to L (8 credits/hr) — halves the credit rate, and since Snowflake auto-scales a single warehouse vertically on demand, all three workloads will still complete within their SLA windows

Use Snowflake's multi-cluster warehouse with min=1, max=4, and auto-suspend at 30 min — the cluster scales from 1 to 4 nodes during peak load and suspends during idle, combining all three workloads without performance degradation
explanation:
Option A is correct. Separate warehouses sized for each workload's actual needs, combined with aggressive auto-suspend, minimizes idle credit burn while preserving performance isolation.

Sizing rationale:
- Analyst (L): L handles interactive queries; 5-minute auto-suspend catches the gap between bursts without leaving the warehouse running all day.
- Batch (XL): XL is appropriate for dbt's parallel model runs; scheduled resume at 10 PM avoids the 30-second cold-start on the first job; 10-minute suspend prevents idle credits between jobs in the batch window.
- BI (XS): XS is sufficient for 15–30 second refreshes on pre-built queries; 2-minute auto-suspend ensures the warehouse suspends between 5-minute refresh cycles (5 min interval − 30 sec query = 4.5 min idle > 2 min suspend threshold).

Estimated cost: Analyst L ~$7,200/month + Batch XL ~$8,640/month + BI XS ~$130/month ≈ $16,000/month vs $45,000 (~64% savings).

Option B (auto-suspend at 60 min) helps but the 60-minute window means the warehouse stays running for 60 minutes after the last analyst query each evening — still wastes hours of nightly idle at XL rate. Mixing BI refreshes with batch also causes resource contention.

Option C (downsize to L) does not address idle time and incorrectly claims Snowflake scales vertically within a single warehouse — Snowflake scales horizontally (multi-cluster), not vertically.

Option D (multi-cluster) is designed for concurrency bursts (many simultaneous users), not for isolating workload types with different compute needs. It cannot suspend credits for one workload pattern while another runs.
hints: The biggest cost driver is idle time on an expensive warehouse. What is the nightly idle duration, and how much does that cost at XL rates with no auto-suspend?
Auto-suspend reduces idle cost, but the suspend window must be shorter than the gap between queries. What is the gap between BI dashboard refreshes?
Separate warehouses let you right-size each workload independently — a 30-second BI refresh does not need the same compute as a 90-minute dbt run.

title: BigQuery Cost Reduction: Partitioning, Incremental Exports, and Scan Optimization
scenario_context:
A company's BigQuery bill is $38,000/month (on-demand at $5/TB scanned). Usage breakdown:
  - Analyst ad-hoc queries: avg 2 TB/query, 200 queries/day — $2,000/day
  - Daily full export to GCS: SELECT * FROM events (8 TB table, full scan every night) — $40/day
  - Dashboard queries: 500/day, avg 400 GB scanned each — $1,000/day

The events table columns: event_id, user_id, event_type, event_timestamp, properties (JSON), created_date (DATE). No partitioning or clustering is applied. All analyst queries filter on created_date and event_type.
description: Which set of changes has the largest combined cost impact?
options: Partition events by created_date and cluster by event_type: analyst and dashboard queries filtering on created_date will scan only matched partitions (typically 1–7 days of a 3-year table = ~0.1–0.5% of data); replace the nightly full export with an incremental export of only the new partition (~7 GB vs 8 TB); total scan reduction: ~95–99% across all workloads

Enable BigQuery BI Engine for the dashboard workload: BI Engine caches dashboard query results in memory and serves them at near-zero scan cost; the $800/month flat fee recovers cost in the first month since dashboard queries account for $30,000/month
Switch all workloads from on-demand to flat-rate reservations at the 2,000 slot tier ($10,000/month flat): the current $38,000/month on-demand bill makes the commitment immediately cost-effective

Materialize analyst queries as scheduled query results into a summary table updated nightly; analysts query the summary table (KB, not TB) instead of raw events — eliminates ad-hoc scan cost without changing the underlying table structure
explanation:
Option A (partition + cluster + incremental export) has the highest impact because it reduces bytes scanned across all three workloads simultaneously.

Partitioning by created_date means a query filtering `WHERE created_date = '2024-01-15'` scans only 1 day of a 3-year table. If analysts typically filter to 1–7 days, scanned data drops from 2 TB to ~2–14 GB per query (99%+ reduction). Dashboard queries filtering to the last day drop from 400 GB to ~400 MB each. The incremental export replaces an 8 TB nightly full-table scan with a single-partition export of ~7 GB (1 day of data), reducing export cost from $40/day to ~$0.035/day.

Option B (BI Engine) addresses only the dashboard workload and only partially — BI Engine caches query results, not raw table scans; queries that touch non-cached columns still scan. It does not touch analyst or export costs.

Option C (flat-rate reservations) converts variable scan cost to a fixed slot commitment — cheaper than $38,000 on-demand, but it does not reduce bytes scanned. If queries are poorly written and scan more data, the fixed rate advantage erodes. Partitioning reduces the actual work done, benefiting both on-demand and flat-rate pricing.

Option D (summary table) helps analysts but does not reduce export costs or dashboard scan costs, and adds an engineering maintenance burden.
hints: BigQuery charges for bytes scanned, not rows returned. What fraction of an 8 TB table does a query with a date filter on a date-partitioned table actually scan?
The nightly full export scans the entire 8 TB table. How much data does an incremental export (new partition only) scan instead?
Which change reduces bytes scanned across the most workloads simultaneously?

title: Schema Drift Incident: Containment and Forward-Fix Strategy
scenario_context: At 6:14 AM, a Spark batch pipeline fails with: `AnalysisException: cannot resolve 'customer_id' given input columns`. Investigation reveals the upstream MySQL source renamed the column from `customer_id` to `cust_id` at 5:00 AM without notifying the data team. The pipeline runs every hour and has failed 2 consecutive runs. Downstream BI dashboards that read from the pipeline's output table have been dark since 6:14 AM. Pipeline path: MySQL → Spark → Parquet (landing zone) → dbt (staging) → BI dashboards.
description: What is the correct sequence of immediate containment actions followed by the permanent forward-fix?
options: Immediate: (1) Disable the hourly pipeline trigger to stop further failed runs; (2) re-point the dbt staging model to the last successful Parquet output (5:00 AM run, before the rename) — dashboards recover from last-good data; Permanent fix: (3) add a column alias at the MySQL ingestion layer (`cust_id AS customer_id`) to insulate the pipeline from source renames; (4) add a schema contract test that asserts `customer_id` is present in the ingested schema and fails fast before writing any data

Immediate: (1) Contact the upstream MySQL team and ask them to revert the column rename; (2) once reverted, re-enable the pipeline — dashboards recover automatically on the next successful run; Permanent fix: (3) add a Slack channel for upstream teams to announce schema changes in advance

Immediate: (1) Manually edit the dbt staging model to read `cust_id` instead of `customer_id`; (2) re-run the hourly pipeline immediately — it will succeed with the renamed column; Permanent fix: (3) document the column rename in the data catalog

Immediate: (1) Scale the Spark cluster to 4× its normal size to process the backlog of 2 missed hourly runs faster; (2) re-enable the trigger once caught up; Permanent fix: (3) add monitoring on the pipeline's dashboard refresh latency so future outages are detected faster
explanation:
Option A is correct. The containment + forward-fix strategy follows the principle: stop the bleeding first, restore service from last-known-good state, then fix the root cause permanently.

Immediate actions:
1. Disable the trigger — a pipeline failing every hour generates alert fatigue and obscures signal. Stopping it prevents further failures while the fix is applied.
2. Re-point dbt to last-good Parquet — the 5:00 AM run succeeded (before the rename), so the Parquet landing zone contains valid data. Re-pointing dbt to this snapshot restores dashboards in minutes without waiting for a pipeline fix or a MySQL revert.

Permanent fix:
3. Column alias at ingest — `SELECT cust_id AS customer_id` in the MySQL reader layer decouples all downstream models from the source's column naming. When the source renames a column again, the alias is the single change point.
4. Schema contract test — a pre-write assertion that `customer_id` is present in the ingested DataFrame fails fast with a clear error before any Parquet is written with corrupt schema, preventing the silent 2-run failure window.

Option B (ask MySQL team to revert) depends on an external team responding at 6:14 AM. Even if they agree, the revert can take hours, extending the dashboard outage unnecessarily.

Option C (edit dbt staging to use cust_id) is a quick fix that re-exposes the same fragility. If the source renames again, every dbt model referencing the column must be updated. The fix belongs in the ingestion layer.

Option D (scale the cluster) misdiagnoses the problem. The failures are a schema mismatch, not a throughput issue. More compute does not fix an AnalysisException.
hints: When a pipeline fails due to a breaking schema change, the first priority is stopping further failed runs and restoring dashboards from the last valid data — not necessarily fixing the pipeline immediately.
Where in the pipeline is the best place to absorb source schema changes? The ingestion layer or the transformation layer?
A schema contract test at the start of the pipeline catches schema drift before any data is written to the landing zone.

title: CDC Watermark Too Short — Late Debezium Events Silently Dropped
scenario_context: A Flink streaming job joins CDC events from Debezium with a dimension table. Consumer lag on the CDC topic is consistently 0. Despite this, events with event_ts values between 02:03 AM and 02:04 AM are missing from the output mart every night. Investigation shows that MySQL I/O contention during a nightly index rebuild causes Debezium to buffer CDC events for 3–8 minutes before publishing them. The Flink watermark is set to 2 minutes.
description: Why are the 02:03–02:04 AM events silently dropped, and what is the correct fix?
options: The watermark (2 min) is shorter than the CDC lag spike (3–8 min): by the time Debezium publishes an event timestamped 02:03 AM, Flink's watermark has already advanced past 02:05+ AM, so the event is classified as late and dropped. Fix: increase the watermark to at least 10 minutes, or route late events to a side output for batch correction
Consumer lag of 0 proves all events are being consumed; the missing rows are caused by a Flink state backend TTL expiring before the join completes. Fix: increase the state TTL beyond 8 minutes

Debezium's MySQL connector filters out events that arrive during I/O contention windows. Fix: configure Debezium's heartbeat interval to be shorter than the contention window so the connector stays healthy
The missing events have event_ts values that fall outside the Flink job's allowed processing-time window. Fix: switch the join to processing-time semantics to avoid event-time ordering constraints
explanation: Consumer lag measures how far behind the Kafka consumer is from the latest offset — it does not measure how long Debezium took to publish the event. During MySQL I/O contention, Debezium buffers internally and publishes a burst of events late. When Flink finally receives an event timestamped 02:03 AM, its event-time watermark has already advanced to 02:05+ AM (driven by events from other partitions that arrived on time). Because 02:03 is behind the watermark, Flink classifies the event as late and drops it silently — no errors are raised. The fix is a watermark large enough to cover the observed CDC lag spike. A 10-minute watermark (covering the 8-minute worst case with 2 minutes of buffer) ensures the event is still within the allowed lateness window when it arrives. Alternatively, side-output routing captures late events for batch reconciliation without dropping them. Option B misidentifies the cause — state TTL is about how long Flink holds unmatched state for a join, not about event ordering. Option C is wrong — Debezium does not filter events during contention; it buffers them. Option D loses event-time ordering guarantees and would cause incorrect join results when events from different partitions arrive out of order.
hints: In event-time processing, 'progress' is tracked by a mechanism that advances based on observed timestamps plus a configurable tolerance. What determines when that mechanism advances past a given event time — and what does consumer lag tell you about when events were published?

A watermark of 2 minutes means Flink will drop any event whose event_ts is more than 2 minutes behind the current watermark. If Debezium delays publishing by 3–8 minutes, what happens to those events when they finally arrive?

title: Dynamic Partition Overwrite Deleting the Entire Table
scenario_context: A daily Spark batch job writes to a Hive-partitioned Parquet table using `.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("event_date").parquet(output_path)`. On the first run after the cluster was rebuilt, the job processes only today's partition — but the entire output_path is wiped, deleting 18 TB of historical partitions. The job completed successfully with no errors.
description: Why was the entire table deleted instead of just today's partition, and what is the correct fix?
options: The default Spark behavior for mode("overwrite") with partitionBy is STATIC partition overwrite: Spark deletes the entire output path before writing, regardless of which partitions are in the current batch. The cluster rebuild reset spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode to its default (STATIC). Fix: set spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode=DYNAMIC so Spark deletes only the partitions present in the current write

The job used .parquet(output_path) instead of saveAsTable(), which bypasses Hive Metastore partition tracking and always performs a full-path overwrite. Fix: switch to df.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("schema.table_name") to enable partition-level overwrite

mode("overwrite") combined with partitionBy always performs a full-path overwrite in Spark — this is by design to ensure idempotency. Fix: switch to mode("append") with a pre-step that deletes only today's partition before writing
The cluster rebuild installed a newer version of Spark that changed the overwrite behavior. Fix: pin the Spark version to the previous release and rerun the job
explanation: Spark's default partitionOverwriteMode is STATIC. In STATIC mode, `.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy(...)` deletes the entire output path (all partitions) before writing the new data — it does not limit the delete scope to only the partitions present in the current DataFrame. This is a well-known footgun: the job succeeds, the logs show no errors, but all partitions not in the current batch are silently wiped. DYNAMIC mode (`spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode=DYNAMIC`) scopes the overwrite to only the partitions actually written by the current job — partitions not in the current batch are left untouched. On a rebuilt cluster, this setting reverts to the default (STATIC) unless it is set in the job's SparkConf or the cluster baseline config. Option B is incorrect — saveAsTable() vs .parquet() does not determine the overwrite scope in the way described; the partitionOverwriteMode setting governs this for both. Option C is incorrect — mode("overwrite") with DYNAMIC correctly limits deletion to current-batch partitions; it is not inherently a full-path operation. Option D is incorrect — this is not a version change; STATIC is the default across Spark versions.
hints: Spark has two partition overwrite modes: STATIC and DYNAMIC. What does STATIC mode delete when you call mode("overwrite").partitionBy("event_date")?

The cluster was rebuilt and the job ran without errors but wiped 18 TB. What configuration setting controls whether overwrite deletes the entire output path or only the partitions in the current write?

title: Schema Merge Upcasting Numeric Column to String Across Parquet Sources
scenario_context: A Spark job reads 203 Parquet files from a data lake using spark.read.option("mergeSchema", "true").parquet(lake_path). Downstream aggregations on the order_total column fail with: AnalysisException: cannot resolve 'SUM(order_total)' due to data type mismatch: argument 1 requires double type, however, 'order_total' is of string type. Investigation shows 192 files have order_total as DOUBLE and 11 files (written by service_b last week) have order_total as STRING.
description: Why does mergeSchema produce a STRING column type instead of DOUBLE, and what is the correct fix?
options: With mergeSchema=true, Spark resolves type conflicts by promoting to the most permissive common type. STRING can represent any value (including doubles), so Spark upcasts DOUBLE → STRING rather than downcasting STRING → DOUBLE (which would be lossy). Fix: correct the service_b writer to produce DOUBLE, or cast order_total to DOUBLE at read time using .withColumn("order_total", col("order_total").cast("double"))

mergeSchema=true only merges column additions (new columns), not type conflicts. When a type conflict is detected, Spark falls back to the last-written schema (the service_b STRING files), overwriting the majority DOUBLE type. Fix: disable mergeSchema and use schema enforcement instead
The 11 STRING files corrupt the schema registry entry for order_total. Fix: delete the 11 service_b files and rewrite them with the correct DOUBLE type before re-reading the lake path
Spark's majority-wins schema resolution would choose DOUBLE (192 files) over STRING (11 files). This behavior indicates a Spark version bug. Fix: upgrade to the latest Spark patch version
explanation: Spark's mergeSchema resolves type conflicts by choosing the most permissive compatible type, not the majority type. Between DOUBLE and STRING, STRING is more permissive — every DOUBLE value can be represented as a STRING, but not every STRING can be safely cast to DOUBLE. Spark therefore promotes all order_total values to STRING across all 203 files, even though 94% of files use DOUBLE. This is a widening type promotion, not a majority vote. The 11 service_b files act as a type anchor that pulls the entire merged schema to STRING. The correct fix is upstream: the service_b writer should produce DOUBLE. As a read-time workaround, casting order_total back to DOUBLE works if the STRING values are valid numeric representations, but this masks the root cause and will silently fail if any STRING values are non-numeric. Option B is incorrect — mergeSchema does handle type conflicts (via promotion), not just column additions, and it does not use last-written-schema as a fallback. Option C is incorrect — deleting the files is destructive and addresses the symptom, not the root cause in the service_b writer. Option D is incorrect — this is documented Spark behavior, not a bug.
hints: mergeSchema resolves type conflicts by finding the most permissive common type, not by majority vote. Between DOUBLE and STRING, which type can represent all values of the other?
If Spark chose DOUBLE as the merged type for order_total, what would happen to the 11 STRING files where order_total contains values that aren't valid numbers?

title: Sink-Side I/O Backpressure Causing Unbounded State Accumulation
scenario_context: A Flink streaming job reads from Kafka and writes enriched records to a JDBC sink. Over 72 hours, the job's managed state grows from 2 GB to 14 GB, then the TaskManager is OOMKilled. The Kafka consumer lag remains at 0 throughout. Sink JDBC write latency starts at 3 ms/record, then degrades to 220 ms/record over the same 72-hour window as the downstream database load increases. The job uses a synchronous JDBC writer backed by a LinkedBlockingQueue with no capacity limit.
description: What is the root cause of the unbounded state growth, and what is the correct architectural fix?
options: The synchronous JDBC writer is slower than the Kafka source rate as write latency degrades. Because the LinkedBlockingQueue is unbounded, the operator buffers records without limit rather than applying backpressure to the Kafka consumer. Over 72 hours, the queue grows to fill available heap. Fix: bound the queue capacity and configure Flink's network buffer backpressure to propagate upstream — when the sink is saturated, the Kafka consumer naturally slows, preventing unbounded accumulation

The Flink state backend TTL is not configured, so all keyed state accumulates indefinitely regardless of sink latency. Fix: set a state TTL equal to the maximum expected event lateness so state is evicted after records are processed

The OOMKill is caused by the Kafka consumer pulling records faster than the JVM can garbage-collect the deserialized objects. Fix: reduce the Kafka fetch.max.bytes setting to limit the volume of data pulled per poll cycle

The JDBC connection pool is exhausted after 72 hours of continuous writes, causing new write attempts to block indefinitely and accumulate in heap. Fix: increase the JDBC connection pool size to match the sink parallelism
explanation: The root cause is a missing backpressure boundary between the Kafka source and a degrading synchronous sink. As the downstream database slows from 3 ms to 220 ms per write, the JDBC writer's throughput drops ~73x. The Kafka consumer, however, continues reading at full rate because consumer lag is 0 — it is not being slowed down by the sink. The unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue absorbs the throughput gap: records pile up in the queue faster than they are drained. Over 72 hours, this gap compounds into 12 GB of heap-resident records. The fix is two-part: (1) bound the queue so that when it fills, the enqueue call blocks; (2) ensure Flink's network backpressure mechanism propagates that blocking signal upstream to the Kafka source operator, which then slows its consumption rate. This is the standard backpressure pattern for protecting streaming jobs from degrading sinks. Option B is partially related (state TTL is a useful general practice) but the state described here is buffered sink records, not keyed operator state — TTL does not evict queue contents. Option C is incorrect — the problem is write throughput, not GC pressure from deserialization. Option D is incorrect — pool exhaustion would cause write errors, not silent queue growth; JDBC pool size is a concurrency setting, not a throughput fix.
hints: Consumer lag = 0 means Kafka is keeping up. If the sink is slowing down but the source is not, where does the throughput gap accumulate?
An unbounded queue between a fast producer and a slow consumer will fill indefinitely. What mechanism prevents the queue from growing without bound?

title: Warehouse Cost Spike: Dashboard Refresh Rate Preventing Auto-Suspend
scenario_context: A company's Snowflake bill for REPORT_WH (Large, auto-suspend set to 5 minutes) jumps from $1,700/month to $37,300/month over a single billing cycle. Query volume on REPORT_WH increased from 8,400 to 142,000 queries/month. The warehouse is used exclusively by a BI dashboard tool. The dashboard was unchanged; only the number of subscribed users grew from 40 to 680. No new dashboards were added.
description: What is the most likely root cause of the 22× cost increase, and what is the correct fix?
options: The BI dashboard tool refreshes all subscribed dashboards on a per-user schedule.
